reference.source: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases / CDC guidance
clinicalPearls: A mosquito-borne alphavirus of Central and South America and occasionally the southern United States, with rodents as enzootic reservoirs and epizootic strains amplified in horses
In contrast to eastern equine encephalitis, most human infections cause a self-limiting acute febrile illness with headache, myalgia, and prostration rather than encephalitis
A minority, particularly children, develop neuroinvasive disease with seizures and encephalitis; overall mortality is much lower than for eastern equine encephalitis
Large epizootics in horses, which suffer high mortality and amplify the virus, typically precede and predict human outbreaks
The virus is highly infectious as an aerosol, making it a recognised laboratory-acquired infection hazard requiring enhanced biosafety
Management is supportive with no licensed specific antiviral; equine vaccination and mosquito control are central to outbreak prevention
Diagnosis uses RT-PCR early and serology (IgM) thereafter, interpreted with the mosquito-exposure and equine-outbreak history
reference.pathophysiology: Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus circulates in enzootic cycles between rodents and mosquitoes, while epizootic variants replicate to high titres in horses that serve as amplifying hosts and drive outbreaks. Following a mosquito bite the virus replicates in lymphoid tissue and produces viraemia, giving rise to a systemic febrile illness. Neuroinvasion occurs in a subset of patients, with the virus infecting neurons and provoking inflammation, but central nervous system involvement is less frequent and generally less devastating than in eastern equine encephalitis. Its efficient aerosol infectivity accounts for the laboratory-acquired infection risk.
additionalDifferentials: Dengue and other arboviral febrile illnesses
Other equine encephalitides (eastern and western equine encephalitis)
Influenza and nonspecific viral febrile illness
additionalInvestigations: RT-PCR on blood for viral RNA during the acute viraemic phase
Serum and cerebrospinal fluid IgM serology
Full blood count often showing leucopenia
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis when encephalitis is suspected
Neuroimaging in patients with neurological features
Testing to exclude co-endemic febrile illnesses such as dengue and malaria
redFlags: Seizures or declining consciousness signalling neuroinvasive disease, especially in children
Rapid clinical deterioration during an active equine epizootic
Laboratory exposure raising concern for aerosol-acquired infection
reference.prognosis: Most patients recover fully from the febrile illness; neuroinvasive disease is uncommon and carries a lower fatality than eastern equine encephalitis, though children with encephalitis may have neurological sequelae.
pitfalls: Assuming encephalitis is the usual presentation when most cases are a self-limiting febrile illness
Neglecting aerosol biosafety precautions in the laboratory
Overlooking the predictive value of concurrent equine outbreaks
Failing to distinguish it from dengue and other co-endemic arboviral fevers
Underestimating neuroinvasive risk in paediatric patients
